title: Money Stuff: Nvidia’s Board Had to Do Something
contentHtml:
Oh Jensen

Someone once told me that the G in ESG is there to make the numbers work. If you are an environmental investor, sometimes you put environmental concerns above shareholder returns. If you are a social investor, sometimes you put social concerns above shareholder returns. Governance is different: Governance means making sure that the managers of a company put shareholder returns above their own interests. If environmental, social and governance investing has good performance — if ESG stocks go up — it stands to reason that a lot of that performance would come from the governance.

I don’t really want to argue for this analysis, which is debatable in various ways,[1] but there is something to it. “Governance” is, traditionally, about shareholder value, about how the profits of a company are split between its managers and its owners. Finance and legal academics noticed that, if a company makes a lot of money, the bandits in charge of the company could keep all the money for themselves and not give any of it to shareholders. “The premise behind modern corporate finance in general,” writes Jean Tirole on the first page of Chapter 1 of his corporate finance textbook, “is that corporate insiders need not act in the best interests of the providers of the funds.” Governance is about keeping an eye on the managers, so they do not become bandits, so the shareholders can get some of the money.

This works very well in textbooks, but in the real world you have to take account of the particular skills and characteristics of particular bandits. Every so often, Elon Musk will go to the board of directors of Tesla Inc. and hint “hey, nice company you have here, it would be a shame if I were to go build robots elsewhere and break some stuff on my way out,” and the board will give him an extra trillion dollars. Banditry! But the shareholders do not complain, much, because Musk’s idiosyncratic personal involvement really is crucial to Tesla being worth a trillion dollars in the first place. They do complain a little, so this year Musk took SpaceX public with a governance structure that gives him complete control forever and prohibits shareholders from complaining. This is very bad governance. Theory would tell you that you should avoid Musk and SpaceX and invest your money with some other equivalently talented and motivated rocket entrepreneur who has built a $2 trillion rocket/AI company with better shareholder rights. But good luck finding that company!

In theory, good governance is about increasing shareholder returns, supervising executives and making sure that their interests are aligned with those of shareholders. In practice, shareholder returns often come from weirdos who do stuff for their own reasons and don’t react well to supervision. In practice, boards of directors sometimes do need to choose between good governance and shareholder returns. Which is weird because the point of the good governance is the shareholder returns.

You know who turned out to be a bandit?

Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, the preeminent face of the AI infrastructure boom, was ousted from his post after reports of two affairs, including with one woman who is suspected of spying for China.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. The board, which has never had a chair before, appointed Harvey Jones, 73, to the role. Jones, who has been on the board for years, formerly led Synopsys Inc., a company that Nvidia last year took a $2 billion stake in.

Nvidia shares fell more than 11% to $155.13. Its market capitalization slipped $450 billion.

In a sense, there are two governance stories here. One happened this week, when Nvidia’s board was faced with the choice between:

  • Keeping Huang as CEO, even after he did a more or less unforgivable assortment of bad things; or
  • Firing him and more or less certainly destroying shareholder value, at least in the short run.

They chose to fire him, and the stock went down. It has recovered a bit: As of noon today, Nvidia’s stock was down about 4.9%, for a market cap of a bit less than $4 trillion. That’s down about $200 billion from yesterday, when Huang was still the CEO, and down almost a trillion dollars from last Tuesday. Huang is an unusually hands-on CEO who was critical to Nvidia’s success, and when the first affair news broke, I just assumed he was essential to the company and its business. “Maybe the board will actually fire him even though he is irreplaceable, and Nvidia’s performance will suffer,” I wrote, citing other analysts who said things like “Nvidia is almost completely dependent on him” and “no one yet can imagine separating Huang from Nvidia.” “‘As a student of economic history, I don’t know if there’s ever been such a key man holding so much of this industry up,’ Blue Bear Capital investor Thomas Ferguson said” yesterday. But now he’s out, and shareholders, as expected, were sad.

At least in the short run. In the longer run, arguably Huang created Nvidia’s culture in his own image, and the culture — rather than his personal efforts — will keep the company humming:

“The fundamentals of the business (if not the leadership) are clearly still intact with numbers that remain massive (and probably still headed higher),” Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, said in a note late Wednesday. “We don’t think the company should have huge issues operating while engaged in a search for new leadership.”

And you could tell stories like “Nvidia will have an easier time persuading regulators to let it sell chips abroad with a non-spy-tainted CEO,” though it’s not clear that’s true. And possibly visionary CEOs are overrated in general. “The graveyards are filled with indispensable men,” Lloyd Blankfein tweeted this morning.

The other, bigger governance story happened over the last decade or so, when Nvidia’s board was faced with a continuing slow-moving choice between:

  • Letting Huang run the company with “total control,” intense personal attention to everything, 60 direct reports and no succession plan; or
  • Thinking a bit harder about governance.

If you are the board of directors of a mature $4 trillion company, what you want, when you discover that your CEO is having affairs with customers and employees and maybe involved an espionage situation, is to be able to get rid of him. You want that decision to be easy and minimally destructive. You want a deep bench of possible successors, a clear org chart that a new CEO can manage, a company that can run on its own without its visionary CEO making every decision. “Huang has used the structure of the company as a way to make himself hard to fire,” writes Byrne Hobart, and that’s the bad governance.

It’s hard, of course. There were no good answers for the board this week, or 10 years ago. Nvidia’s stock returned 700,000% during Huang’s tenure as CEO, and arguably a lot of that is because of his intense and personalistic management style. A board that pushed Huang, over the years, to run the company more normally might have given up a lot of shareholder value; it might have turned Nvidia into a normal company, in a bad way. But the result is that Nvidia had a hard-to-fire CEO and had to fire him. And that’s not great for shareholders either.

Meanwhile there’s an Anthropic IPO

On the one hand this is very normal, the standard IPO playbook:

Anthropic’s bankers are weighing plans to increase the AI group’s initial public offering price after receiving heavy demand from investors, less than a day after disclosing that it would target a $1.4tn valuation when it lists next week.

Bankers have indicated they expect to raise the share price above the $70-$78 range announced in a filing early on Tuesday, which could increase the valuation target to $1.5tn or more in the coming days, according to five people familiar with the matter.

A boost in the share price would also increase the total funds raised in the IPO beyond $100bn. Three of the company’s backers said Anthropic was now focused on raising as much as possible via the listing to support its heavy spending on computing power, rather than maximising its valuation.

You launch at a conservative valuation, you get investors excited at the prospect of a bargain, the orders pour in, the deal is oversubscribed, you raise the marketing range and price into strong demand to get a nice IPO pop. Everything is going as planned.

On the other hand, it is very funny that arguably the most important IPO of the artificial intelligence era — the most important IPO in human history??? — happened to launch into the Jensen Huang Affair Tape. Like the executive team shows up at an investor meeting prepared to talk about revenue growth and compute costs and ushering in an age of miracles while heading off human extinction, and the investors are like “did you hear he had a different affair? With his direct report?” and then their phones buzz and they say “oh no he resigned!” and the executive team is like “wait really?” and the investors are like “can you believe it” and the executive team is like “our revenue is growing at a” and the investors are like “shhh hang on a minute I gotta look at the memes.” It’s not a great backdrop for an AI IPO, but it’s not a terrible one either; it’s just weird. Just a lot going on.

I find something about it …. reassuring? Inspiring? Could a country of geniuses in a data center do that? Anthropic’s IPO suggests the prospect of a post-human future, but there are still some things about humanity that the computers can’t take away from us.

What does ChatGPT tell investors to do?

I have wondered about this for a while. Like, there is some baseline set of retail investor behavior: Some people buy and hold index funds, others have financial advisers who put them into diversified portfolios of stocks and funds and non-traded business development companies, others YOLO meme stock call options, others put their retirement money in a diversified portfolio of sports bets, etc. etc. etc. Some mechanisms — the rising public profile of indexing, 401(k) plan investment defaults, Reddit message boards — cause herding, as many retail investors make correlated investing decisions and end up in the same sorts of investments. Other mechanisms — American individualism, doing your own research, idiosyncratic financial advisers, weird niche Reddit rabbitholes — cause diversity, as many retail investors make uncorrelated investing decisions and end up in weird places on their own.

And then you add modern artificial intelligence. You give retail investors access to large language model chatbots. What happens? You could imagine at least three broad sorts of answers:

  1. More individualism. Everyone has a personalized robot in their pocket that tells them what they want to hear. Chatbots advise retail investors on how to build a portfolio that reflects their particular risk tolerances, social commitments, favorite brands and general sense of whimsy. Instead of buying and holding portfolios of a dozen passive exchange-traded funds, people can do all sorts of active trading strategies; they can describe in plain language the sorts of things they’d like to do, and the chatbots will put together an executable plan. All of these plans will be different, some will sell while others buy, and everyone will end up holding different assets at different times.
  2. More herding toward the standard consensus. There is a standard consensus! Everyone basically knows how retail investors are supposed to invest: diversification, low fees, long holding periods, etc. I am not giving you investing advice, but the standard advice is widely available on the internet. Modern LLMs are machines for reflecting the standard consensus on the internet. Everyone will type into their chatbot “what should I invest in” and the chatbot will be like “duh low-cost diversified index funds.” The problem of what retail investors should invest in is largely solved, and the financial industry has spent much of the last decade un-solving it, but maybe AI will solve it again.
  3. More herding into weird stuff. It’s not impossible that everyone will type into their chatbot “what should I invest in” and the chatbot will be like “duh zero-day options on meme stocks.” Modern LLMs are machines for reflecting the consensus on the internet, but arguably they overweight the consensus on Reddit. It’s possible that the LLMs will have particular stocks and sectors and strategies that they like — because their training data likes those things, or for weirder emergent reasons — and will nudge all of the retail investors into their favored stocks. And then if you know which stocks ChatGPT likes, you buy those stocks, because they have the tailwind of millions of ChatGPT-advised investors also buying them.

Anyway here’s the answer:

Generative AI is a general purpose technology with rapidly growing adoption among retail investors. How does the adoption of this technology change household investment decisions? I study the adoption of a generative AI–based conversational assistant by retail investors, using data that link investors’ prompts and AI answers to transaction-level trading records and portfolio holdings. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, I find that generative AI adoption increases investment in index funds relative to individual stocks by 7.6 percentage points. As a result, AI adoption reduces investors’ return loss, which measures the expected return forgone due to underdiversification at a given level of risk, by 43 basis points on average, with substantial heterogeneity across investors. Less diversified portfolios improve the most, with return loss declining by 101 basis points.

That’s from “Generative AI and Retail Investment,” by Valerie Baldinger of New York University, via the Substack of her adviser, Arpit Gupta. It’s Answer 2: There’s a standard consensus about how retail investors should invest, the chatbots tell the retail investors to do the standard consensus and, interestingly, the investors do it. Apparently the chatbots are persuasive because they listen deeply to the investors, consider their particular financial situations, optimize for their hopes and dreams, and then say “just index bro” but in a personalized way. Baldinger:

I provide evidence on personalization as a mechanism through which generative AI affects investment behavior. Personalization is a key attraction of generative AI chatbots and has been explored in the nudge literature as a way of altering behavior (DellaVigna and Linos, 2022). I find that investors are more likely to implement recommendations when answers use more personal details. ... I find that a one-standard-deviation increase in portfolio personalization raises implementation by 11.9 percentage points. Personalization relies on personal data that allow chatbots and AI agents to tailor their responses to consumers’ circumstances, so this finding also has important implications for the value of data in the age of AI.

Gupta writes: “They give people detailed reasoning chains which reference their individual stock holdings to justify why they should buy index funds, and this really persuades people.” That really is the core job of a financial adviser! Listen to your clients, evaluate their risk tolerances, consider their particular circumstances and then put them into low-cost index funds. It’s nice that the chatbots can do it.

Head of Macro

We have talked a few times about James Fishback, who became famous by going around telling everyone that he was the “Head of Macro” at Greenlight Capital, and then suing Greenlight when it said he wasn’t. He has since moved on to various other endeavors in the same basic field of trolling, like sort of running for governor of Florida. But he has still spent a lot of time on his first love, suing and being sued by Greenlight over the “Head of Macro” stuff. It has not gone well for him. We talked last year about a settlement of one of those lawsuits, in which Fishback admitted that he and his father were copying Greenlight’s trades in their personal accounts. And this week Greenlight founder David Einhorn posted the conclusion of the story on X:

Greenlight has won all litigation with James Fishback. @jamesfishback has been ordered to return every penny of salary and bonus that we ever paid him, to repay the money we lent him, to pay most of our legal fees, and to stop claiming titles, roles and responsibilities he never had. No, Fishback was not the “Head of Macro.” Rather, as the arbitrator found, he was a “faithless servant.”

That’s a fancy legal way of saying that Fishback was so disloyal during his employment that he was ordered to refund to us his entire compensation during his tenure at Greenlight.

The best part might be that the whole “Head of Macro” lawsuit was a set-up:

Fishback and his father concocted a scheme to use a fake reference check to create his fraudulent defamation claim against us.

In September of 2023, after his employment ended, Fishback texted his father a draft of a fake reference check email that included an inquiry as to Fishback’s duties as Greenlight’s “Head of Macro.” In the same chain, Fishback texted his father:

“We need them to DEFAME us. Which THEY WILL. That’s another $1 MM right there.”

Fishback persuaded a friend of a friend who worked at an investment firm to send us the fake reference check. When we responded that Fishback was not the Head of Macro, Fishback promptly sued us, claiming that our response caused the friend’s company to walk away from making a $5 million investment in Fishback’s start-up hedge fund.

The friend of the friend testified under oath that he sent the fake reference check as a favor and that his company was never considering investing with Fishback. The friend got fired.

It was all a sham to conjure a fake legal claim to extract money from us.

Terrific. I assume he’ll be president one day.

[1] First of all, I have not looked at which ESG factors are empirically correlated with higher returns, so I can’t vouch for this theory. More important, the claim that “if you are an environmental investor, sometimes you put environmental concerns above shareholder returns,” etc., is not how most ESG investors would actually describe what they do. ESG investors would say, no, ESG is about identifying particular risk factors that affect long-term shareholder returns; it’s not about putting the environment above shareholder returns but rather about identifying which companies will underperform for environmental reasons. Not everyone believes this, it’s extensively debated, and it’s not that relevant to our current concerns.
